question.text: If USD/INR moves from 82.00 to 84.50, by what percentage has the USD/INR rate increased (measured using the old rate as the denominator, i.e. the conventional INR-depreciation measure from the USDINR rate)?

explanation.text: The Logic: Percentage increase in USD/INR using the old rate as the denominator = (New - Old)/Old x 100 = (84.50 - 82.00)/82.00 x 100 = 2.50/82.00 x 100 = 3.0488%, or approximately 3.05%. This measures the percentage rise in the USD/INR rate itself, which is the conventional way the workbook reports INR depreciation against USD. The Trap: Option B (2.96%) uses the new rate as the denominator (2.50/84.50), which corresponds to the fall in INR value measured in USD terms, not the rise in USD/INR. Option C (2.50%) ignores the denominator and just states the rupee-point change. Option D (3.50%) is an arithmetic distractor. In the original ambiguous version the stem said "INR depreciated against USD" without specifying which percentage-denominator convention to use, so both 3.05% (USDINR-rate basis) and 2.96% (INR-value-in-USD basis) were defensible. Note: The original was ambiguous because workbook p.23 supports the directional statement but does not nail down the percentage-denominator convention. The stem has been tightened to specify "increase in USD/INR rate, using the old rate as denominator" so that option A is uniquely correct. Source: NISM Series I (Currency Derivatives, Dec 2025), pp.23, 100.
